utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you please stand? Would you please read the affirmation on the card that is offered to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next witness deals with the hospital, the JNA barracks, return to the hospital, and in relation to various people who ended up at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, what is your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: My name is Vilhelm, Rudolf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say that you live in Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I live in Vukovar. I have a wife and two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think if I may just tease you slightly, it's an area, I think, that's known as the Hollywood of Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's right to say you have never given evidence before. This is your first time before a court?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: The first time. I have never been convicted, and this is the first time I am testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I am an ethnic Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions, please, about November 1991. The Court have heard a great deal of evidence about the run-up in time through August, September, October, November of 1991, and I don't want to deal with any details there. Can I deal, please, with your leaving your home and going to the Vukovar Hospital? So can we start with your evidence at that particular time? Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's right to say that you went to the hospital on the 17th of November. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why did you go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: The Chetniks were coming from all directions. My wife worked at the hospital. Several days prior to me going to the hospital, we were in a basement in one of Velepromet warehouses. I came to the hospital on the 17th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And who did you go to the hospital with?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I went with my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you went to the hospital, what were the conditions like at that time?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: There was shelling, the city was destroyed, the patients and the wounded were in the corridors of the hospital. My wife and I went to a part of the basement where there was a nun with Dr. Kolak and young children who were patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I just ask you to speak a little more slowly? Because it makes it much easier for the interpreter. Is that all right, you can do that?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, can you remember when the JNA or paramilitaries first came to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: They came for the first time on the 19th in the evening; however, I didn't see them, I only heard this. I saw them myself on the 20th in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal with the morning of the 20th, please? What did you see or who did you see arrive?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I was in the basement where the children were. I was somewhere in the middle of the basement. I heard them say that the soldiers were saying that all of us had to go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you eventually go outside?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: My wife went to the meeting. Since she was a physician, she went to this meeting with all other medical staff. I stayed on for a bit longer and after that I went out through the back door of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who did you go out with?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I went out together with other people who were in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what happened when you went outside by the back door?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: When we went out by the back door, we saw soldiers there. They lined us up against the wall to the left of the door. We had to put our hands on our backs and they started searching us, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you went outside, did men and women remain together?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No. The men were separated to one side, and the women went to another side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And was that a choice that they made, or they were told to line up in that way?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I don't know that. This is how they ordered us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who ordered whom?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: The soldiers told us at the door to line up against the wall and to put our hands up. They searched us to see if we had any weapons on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can I just deal with -- you said that men and women were apart. I just want to deal with the men, if I may.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you went outside, were there any other men who were lined up as well?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No. As they came through the door -- as we came through the door we were told to line up against the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how many people lined up, approximately? Over 100, less than 100? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I can't say the exact number, but based on the fact that three or four buses went to the barracks and each bus carried between 20 and 22 people, then I would say that the total number was between 80 and 90.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's just deal with the buses for a moment. Did you get on any bus at that time?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I was boarded on to the second bus in the way -- in the order that they were lined towards the back door of the hospital, facing the cemetery. I entered the second bus and went to the middle of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just deal with your bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When they had finished loading your bus how many people do you think were on that bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: About 20 to 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how many people would a bus normally hold?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I don't know what the capacity is of each bus, but roughly 20 to 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So are you saying that the bus is almost full or not? Can you just tell us how full the bus was?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Our bus was full. I don't know about other buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's deal with your bus. Were there any women on your bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you recognise some of the people on your bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The people who were with me on the bus, I knew some of them because I was born in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And of the people that you recognised, are you able to say what ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: All of them were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And again, if we deal with the bus, do you know if there were any soldiers on your bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: There was a soldier with a rifle at the door, and I'm not sure about the driver, but I think that he also was in a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if we deal with the soldier with a rifle, are you able to say whether he was a regular soldier or what I will call paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: He was a regular soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And were you told why it was you were going on to the bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Nobody said anything to us. Simply once the buses were loaded, we set out and drove through the centre of the town towards Vasariste or the fair-grounds where the barracks was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us follow that drive, if we may. Did the buses, when the buses were driven away from the hospital, did they stop again?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No. They didn't stop. They drove to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, the barracks, what barracks are they?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: The one and only barracks, which is located at Vasariste, or the fair-grounds. That's the only barracks that exist in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: By those barracks, do you mean JNA barracks or not?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, the JNA barracks where the members of the army were, where they served their military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can I just deal with time for one moment? Here you are, you get on the bus at the hospital. It is then driven to the barracks and it then stops at the barracks. How long do you think it was from getting on your bus until you got to the barracks? I don't mean the drive; I mean from the time that you actually got on and then ended up at the barracks. Can you tell us? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say. I wouldn't be able to give you the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, that's very kind. Can I then deal with the people who were on the bus? I've already dealt with it in one way, but were you able to recognise people on the bus by their names, or did you know the names of some of the people on the bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I knew names of some people. In some cases I knew last names or only first names. In Vukovar we typically know other people's last names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Shall we try the last names first and the first names last, shall we do that? So dealing with the last names, can you tell us, please, some of the last names of people that you recognised as being on your bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I recognised Lovro Barbir, Jakov Simunovic, and Sime Simunovic. Jakov and Sime Simunovic. Medjesi, the father and the son. The son of Pajo Djukic. I know his last name was Djukic. His father was a doctor. And there was a Kolesar there as well. He was my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know anyone called Adzaga?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I do know the person called Adzaga, he was returned to the hospital once. We were sent from the barracks back to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And are you able to say if he was on your bus on the journey from the hospital to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes. He was at the hospital. He was with me. He went to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us you were going to deal with last and first names, but is it right to say those are the only names of the people that you can remember who were on the bus with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I can also remember Josip Zelko whom I also saw on the bus which was sent back to the hospital. There was another man, I don't know his name, however, his wife worked with my wife, and he used to work for Elektroslavonija, which is the electrical power utility company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I just deal with the person called Zeljko? Was he on the bus that travelled - may I just finish? - from the hospital to the barracks or not?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I apologise. It's not Zeljko. It's Zelko, Z-e-l-k-o, Josip Zelko. He was also on the bus. He was returned back to the hospital together with me, and the rest were set free.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But what I am trying to do is just deal with the people who were on the bus who travelled from the hospital to the barracks. I just want to deal with that trip for the moment. We'll deal with any other trips later on. So just focusing on the trip from the hospital to the barracks, you've given us names. What about Zelko? Was he on the bus to the barracks or not?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. With regard to the arrival at the barracks, can you remember if there were any other buses who were present at the barracks when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I didn't see a single bus. I was on the second bus. I don't know exactly how many buses there were, four or five. Those are the buses that drove us from the hospital. They were parked in a semi-circle, one bus behind the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, can we just deal with those buses. You say they were parked in a semi-circle, one behind the other. Can you describe to the court what then happened outside the buses when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Once the buses arrived, about 10 to 12 soldiers and civilians surrounded each bus. They lined up next to each bus, threatening, taking out rifles and pistols, but not shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just want to deal with those people who surrounded each bus. Can we deal just with your bus? Now, when you were on the bus and you arrived at the JNA barracks and you had these 10 to 12 people coming to each bus, what effect did that have on you with them coming, threatening and taking out rifles and pistols?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: All of us were scared. We put our heads down. I don't know if there is a single person who wouldn't be afraid if they saw a rifle or a pistol pointed at them. All of us were terrified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did anyone get on to the bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Not then. Initially nobody got on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Well, not initially, but did anybody then get on the bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: A list came from the hospital, a list of soldiers whose husbands or some other family members worked at the hospital. They wanted their husbands to be sent back to the hospital. The names were read out from that list, and one by one these people transferred to another bus which went to the hospital later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We'll deal with the list in a moment. But can I just deal with the persons that you say you saw outside, 10 to 12 people having rifles and pistols. Did any of them get on to your bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: When the list was completed, the soldiers got on the bus. While we were getting on the bus, a gauntlet was formed so that they beat us on our way to the bus and then also when we were already on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, just before we get to the gauntlet, did you recognise any of the -- either the civilians or the soldiers who were around the bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised one of them. I also recognised one at the reception desk. Since I know almost all people in Vukovar, I recognised Vojnovic, Dule, nicknamed Robija. He is from Negoslavci, and he's not a normal person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's just deal with him. I just want to deal with the bus, please. I don't want to know about the reception desk. I just want to deal with the bus, all right? Now, where did you see him when you were in the bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Right in front of the bus. They were lined up parallel to the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the soldiers that you saw, are you able to say if they were regular soldiers or irregular soldiers? Can you give us an indication of the type of soldier they were?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes. Vojnovic was there, and there were reservists as well as young soldiers. I used to be the warden of the prison in Trpinja so I can tell who is a soldier, who's a sergeant and so on. I had a rank while I served in the army, and I can recognise young conscripts. Young conscripts are orderly. The reservists are older, they are not usually clean shaven. And that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did Robija speak to you at any time?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said, "Ruca, are you an Ustasha too? You will never again be able to fish on the banks of the Danube." I told him I would be back one day but he will then be gone. And this precisely what happened. I thought he was a friend of mine. I used to play football in my time. I play for Rijeka, Borovo and Dinamo Vinkovci. I gave him a hand at the time. He was a pretty good football player himself. I made sure he joined the Borovo club. I gave him his first football boots. I taught him how to catch fish; I gave him my tackle. I had a boat made for him by a friend of mine, and I never saw this coming. I never thought that I would experience this at his hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just deal, then, with the list that you have mentioned? So I just want to ask you questions about this list. The list of names, do you know who was controlling the list at that time?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why do you not know that?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: When I got on to the bus I was scared too. Kept my head down. I wasn't exactly thinking about things like these, who controlled the list. I was the first to get on the bus. I'm talking about the bus that was sent back to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, is it right that you were then taken off the bus or not?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: My name was called out and many others, too, who had previously boarded the buses. We were made to run a gauntlet made up of Chetniks, and people were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say that you were made to run a gauntlet, can you in some detail explain to the Court what you mean by "run a gauntlet"? Run a gauntlet of whom?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I think both soldiers and reservists were there. They were beating the people severely, those people who were trying to reach the bus. They didn't beat me because I was the first to reach the bus, but I was scared out of my wits, so I could hardly remember my own name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what sort of items were they using to beat the people from the bus or being transferred from bus A to another bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Outside the buses they beat us with whatever they could. They kicked us, they hit us, they used their rifle-butts, that sort of thing. On the bus they beat Kolesar and the two Simunovics, as far as I was able to see. They were beating them on the head and wherever they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever see any soldiers or officer or any person stop the beatings of the individuals running through that gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: They were just watching and laughing. Nobody lifted a finger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us about Kolesar. Now, can we just deal with Kolesar? How was he beaten, please?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Kolesar was severely beaten. He said he was an ethnic Ruthenian and that he had nothing to do with this war. And they said, "Yes, yes, you get some too." And they hit him everywhere. They hit him over the head and everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you see any other person being severely beaten?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I didn't see the soldiers, because I was keeping my head down, but I heard both Simunovics moaning and screaming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And were you able to hear any of the words being uttered by the people who were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: The soldiers weren't saying anything at all. They just kept at it. They were beating people. I didn't hear them say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you hear the people who were being beaten say anything?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: They were crying for help. Moaning. Begging to not be beaten anymore. I was scared myself. I didn't utter a word; maybe that was the reason that I was not beaten. But they kept crying for help, they kept saying things, and maybe that was all the more reason for those people to go on beating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You told us that you were the first person to arrive at what I will call the new bus. How many people were transferred to that bus that you went on to?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, 16 or 17 people, the people who were to be sent back to the hospital later on. But at this point we did not yet know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's deal with those 16 or 17 people who go to this new bus. You are at the JNA barracks, you are all on the bus, did it eventually leave the barracks?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, we left the barracks on the bus. We were inside the bus. We left on the bus and the bus drove back to the hospital. It parked outside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal now with your return to the hospital. All right?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you arrived back at the hospital, did you remain on the bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: When we arrived back at the hospital we were ordered to get off the bus and line up. Our wives were waiting for us, or whoever it was who had told them to bring our people back to the hospital. We lined up at the ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you recognise any other people, apart from your family, who were waiting for you?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I recognised the wives of Simunovic, Kolesar, and all those who were waiting there for their husbands to be set free. Biba Kolesar lives on my street. I know her well. Everybody was waiting for their own husbands, sons or whoever was on that bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You told us that you were ordered to get off the bus. Who ordered you to get off the bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I don't know who did, but it must have been one of the soldiers, I assume. Also because Major Sljivancanin was nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you know it was Major Sljivancanin and not some other officer?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I had never seen this comrade, as they would say in the army, at all. I first set eyes on him when I arrived in Zagreb. It was then I first learned that the man's name was Sljivancanin. However, my wife had begged him to help us, and she was the one who told me that that was Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to describe to the Court the height of the man that you say was Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: As tall as I am. Perhaps even taller, give or take an inch or two. Thereabouts. He wore a moustache, a uniform, a cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you saw this man that you call Sljivancanin, were there any other soldiers with him?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: He was with Miroljub Vujovic and Darko Kovacevic, a man better known as Drko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what way were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you were lined up, was that all of you, all the men on the bus who were lined up, or just some?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: All of us. We got off the bus, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what then happened when you were lined up?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: When we were lined up there were Miroljub and Major Sljivancanin, and they asked each man individually whether they were ideologically suitable. Miroljub was pointing fingers at people, and he kept saying, "This one, this one, and this one," and those people would be released. When he came to me, he said that this man had been loyal up to a certain month of the year but that me and my sons where Ustashas, and it was at this point that I was ordered to get back on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you just wait for one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that the interpreters paused when the witness used the following word in the B/C/S, "podoban," p-o-d-o-b-a-n. The interpretation on line -- on page 15, line 16, I don't think is consistent with the meaning of the witness's words. "Ideologically suitable" is the interpretation given, but I think it might be very useful for the witness to explain when Sljivancanin asked Vujovic about whether somebody was "podoban," what exactly did he mean. I don't think the interpretation is quite correct, at least not the way I understand the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how to answer that one, but what he probably had in mind was that up until some months ago I had not opposed the Chetniks. I had been a regular ordinary citizen. Once the war began, I probably switched sides and sided with the Croats. That was probably what he had in mind. I don't know what else to say. A long time ago it was a question of being fit to be a member of the party, of having all the prerequisites for becoming a member of the Communist party, so that is what the word used to apply to or refer to time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am sure my learned friend Mr. Lukic could have asked that question in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But can we just, please, now go right back to what we were asking questions about? That was that were you in a line and you had Major Sljivancanin and Miroljub was pointing people out. So I want you, please, to put your mind back to that piece of evidence that you were giving and tell the Court what was happening when Miroljub was pointing people out.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Miroljub would point people out and these people were free. They would join their wives and go to the other buses. They went one by one, those were who were released. They left with their wives towards the buses parked outside the hospital entrance where the evacuation buses were already lined up. All those who Miroljub Vujovic believed to be Ustashas were taken to one side and sent back to the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can we just deal very slowly, please, because you're still talking very quickly, can we deal slowly, please, with what actually happened to you. What was the conversation with you?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Miroljub told the major that I was an Ustasha and I was sent back to that bus. At this point in time my wife pleaded with Mr. Sljivancanin, Major Sljivancanin to let me go, because I was no Ustasha, she said. She pleaded with all the Serbs she knew and they said, "Maybe tomorrow." But my wife knew that that would be too late for me. A neighbour of mine was a doctor at the hospital, Dr. Stanojevic. She begged him, too, to set me free, to try to get me released, and he said, "Maybe tomorrow," but she knew that would be too late. Still I must say Mr. Stanojevic was married to a Croatian lady. He was a neighbour of mine; he lived two houses further down the street. He went to see a colonel from Belgrade - they were schoolmates, they studied together at university - and that was the reason I was released. It was a soldier who brought a small slip of paper with my name on it. I then got off the bus. I threw myself into my wife's arms, we were crying, and I went to the other side where all those people from the hospital were standing who were preparing to be evacuated to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Again, if I could just ask you to break your answers into smaller parts. Now, let us deal with --

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's all right. Let us deal with the bus itself. Now, you have been placed on the bus. When you were placed on the bus and before you were released from it again - I want to deal with you getting on to the bus or being sent on to the bus - how many people were on that bus? How many men had been put back on?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: There were five or six people who were sent back. I was really scared. My wife said she had never seen me look that way. I probably knew somewhere deep inside that I was being taken away in order to be shot. There was Adzaga there, as well as Josip Zelko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You say that Adzaga was there and Zelko.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I knew both Adzaga and Zelko by sight. I know Adzaga slightly better because he lived on my brother's street. Both he and his brother, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see when they were placed back on the bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No. I left and I later heard that the bus had been driven back to the barracks, or whatever. I don't really know. I myself went elsewhere. And I was happy to have got off that bus, the previous one. I left with my wife, I was the last to board the buses headed for Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I please just ask you to stop again and try and keep your answers shorter. Can I deal with Zelko?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Had he been in the line along with you before being placed back on the bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes. All those from the bus were lined up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And Adzaga, was he in the line with you before he was put back on the bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Adzaga, too, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I want to deal with the other people who were on the bus whose names you do not know. Do you understand whom I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you recognise by face the other people who were put back on the bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I told you I knew almost everybody in Vukovar. But the faces etched in my memory belong to those two people. I was scared out of my wits. I just sat on the front seat of the bus and I kept looking at my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you please -- the question that I have asked is, you have identified two people by name, but there were other people, because you told us there were five or six -- please may I just ask the question? The people who were on the bus whose names you didn't know, had you seen them before? Did you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you pause, please. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. But I think on page 19, lines 5 and 6 and 7 the witness has already answered this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Please carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll ask the question again. You have told us about five or six people being on the bus, two of whom you recognised by name. The other people, did you recognise their faces or not?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I don't remember. As I've said before, I knew nearly everybody in Vukovar, but I don't remember who was on the bus at that time. Or, rather, who else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just deal with one small piece of evidence, and perhaps I should have asked you it before. You told us that you were being taken from the JNA barracks back to the hospital. Do you remember that evidence you gave?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you why it was you were being taken back from the JNA barracks or what was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No one ever told us. We weren't told anything, really. We were all just terrified. Nobody said a word to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. My colleague, Mr. Domazet, will be taking this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told that in actual fact there may be names given, we have one particular name, and it's not on the transcript. Now, if that's the case, I for obvious reasons would want that to be clarified because there is -- it flew on to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there a little arrow-head where the name was put? If that's so, that is followed up afterwards when the tape is checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm told it may be 716, and the names that I have seen and I'm not going to repeat in open court, I do remember him saying, if I may check my own note, I'll see whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: 716. And I have got on my statement, the way I work with my statements, I tick off the names to make sure hopefully that everything is there, and these two names are ticked off as being given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you see the arrow-heads that are there? They are places where those typing and trying to keep up know that they have missed something and it is then checked later and added in. But you might have the witness go over those names again now, just in case, Mr. Moore, before Mr. Domazet continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Forgive me for buckling on that particular suggestion, because I don't want to, as it were, almost impeach my own witness. What I have done in the past, and my learned friends have seen the document, I've given it to them, is I have supplied to the witness the name of the persons named in the back of the indictment and asked him to mark out any of the names of people that he saw on the bus. Now, I would ask that that procedure be adopted rather than ask him to go through what is clearly a very stressful appearance for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, there would be no difficulty from the Tribunal if you want to follow that course. You wouldn't, though, be impeaching your witness if you followed the other course. So whichever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think I will just prefer the documentary course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought you might.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's -- it is on the Sanction. Would Your Honour forgive me a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder if you would be kind enough, Mr. Vilhelm, to look at this particular document.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I can't see that; it's very small print.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I know you're carrying your glasses. No, that won't do. Now, can I just go -- ask you to stop for a moment?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Adzaga.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you just wait for a moment, please, and I will run over this particular document. I think it's right to say that when you were being proofed you were shown a list of names, and these are some of the names, and you have ticked the people that you saw on the bus. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I told you all the people I saw on the bus, those who went to the barracks with me and those who returned to the hospital. I can read out the names of these people one by one, if you'd like me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, I don't want you to do that. But we have a name there of Adzaga. Do you see that name with a tick?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes. Ivan Adzaga.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see him on the bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go down to the next tick?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Lovro Barbir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you see him on the bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, he was an internal inspector. This is a job that I took up during my years as a refugee in the Borovo trading system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But I just want you to answer yes or no when I deal with this list. If I can turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Vladimir Djukic, did you see him on the bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, Vladimir Dzukic. His father was a well-respected specialist at the hospital, a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll turn the page again. And again. Now, can we deal then, please, with the two others. And these are the two that were omitted from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Medjesi, father and son. His nickname was Cigo. He was the head waiter at Grand and at Vucedol. His son was a cafe owner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we go back to the letter D of this list? We can see the name Martin Dosen with an H. Now, did you see Martin Dosen on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I saw Martin Dosen. He was still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where did you see him on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I saw him in front of the hospital entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have no further questions. The two names that were omitted, as far as our records show, are the two Ms. I'm rather surprised my learned friends didn't hear that and help me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to say to my learned friend that we heard these two last names not the first names though.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know their first names. I know that Dzukic was mentioned, and Medjesi, father and son. I don't know their first names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vilhelm. My name is Vladimir Domazet. I'm one of the Defence counsel of Mr. Mrksic, and on behalf of his Defence team I will be putting questions to you. Based on the information you provided to my learned friend, we can see that you were born and raised in Vukovar, that you spent your entire life there. You told the Prosecutor that you lived in a neighbourhood known as Hollywood. Would you please explain to everyone where this neighbourhood is located, this area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Sir, that neighbourhood is located immediately next to the Vuka River. After the bridge the first street that follows is Ivana Gorana Kovacica, and you can recognise it on the basis of a large chimney. We called it Spitznagel. There was a paint store there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let us clarify something at the outset. My learned friend asked you and you confirmed that this is the first time that you are testifying in any trial. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Based on the information I have, you provided a statement to the investigators in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: In Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please wait for the end of my question before answering? This is because of the interpreters. That was sometime in July of 1995; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember how long it took for you to give that statement, how many days?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Just one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: One whole day or less than a day; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Not a whole day. Several hours, a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You must have looked at the statement and then you signed it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Following that did you ever give any other statements to the OTP investigators or in any other proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No. I never gave statements to anyone until I came here to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on that statement, you worked in Borovo as an accountant before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes. During the war -- during the war I worked as an auditor, and before the war I worked in a similar line of work, calculating figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that you worked during the war. Would you please tell us what exactly you had in mind, what period of time and what did you work [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: When we were returned on buses from Sremska Mitrovica, I went to Zagreb and I got hired by Borovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So you are talking about the period after the fall of Vukovar. I thought that you had in mind during the conflict in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, nobody was able to work during the conflict in Vukovar. All of us had to leave our jobs after the month of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I didn't quite understand you because you said "during the war," so I thought that you meant during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Perhaps you misunderstood what I said. While I was an auditor in Zagreb, I went to various stores, and the war was still raging in Zadar and in Dalmatian towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right, all right. You clarified that. When answering one of Mr. Moore's questions you spoke about serving your military service, so I can see that you did that. So would you please give us some details about when, where and which branch of service?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I served in Trebinje in 1960-something, 1965 or 1966. No, it was 1965.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Which branch?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I did not have a rank. But since I was in charge of the football team of the barracks, I was designated to be the prison warden in the north camp in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mean the military prison which existed within the barracks in Trebinje; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You must have been given a rank, such as, for example, lance-corporal or something like that?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, I held no rank. My commander was Colonel Puzigaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you please tell me which arms of service or which branches you served in?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: In the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. After completing your military service you lived in Vukovar. Were you a reservist, did you attend any training, did you have a wartime assignment?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, I did not have any wartime assignments. I was only summoned into the army when the Russians were attacking. I received a call-up to go to a place near Vinkovci. I was there for a month with the JNA as a reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I suppose that you're referring to 1968 when Czechoslovakia was occupied. Is that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I can't remember which year it was, but I spent more than one month in that place near Vinkovci. Can't remember the name of the place. We were in a forest. We had a camp there with tents. We filled various ditches and were creating conditions for us to be able to defend ourselves. That's what they were telling us, that we should be able to defend ourselves in case they attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia? I'm referring now to the time when there was a single-party system?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I was never a member of the party. I was an avid football man, and after completing my work I would go to football practices. My team, Borovo, was in the second league, so I would first work, and then after business hours, would go to football training.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. What about afterwards?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you please tell us something briefly about the situation in Vukovar in early 1991? First of all, tell us, please, did tensions between the Serb and Croat population start escalating at the time and, if so, what is your view about the reasons for that?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Up until the attack when the policemen were killed in Borovo Selo, Serbs and Croats never dreamed that there would be a war. Nobody even considered this as a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. That's not what I had in mind, whether there would be a war or not. Tell us, were there any incidents, were there any explosions, fires, did some people go missing?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Up until that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said yourself that you were not a member of any party; that includes the HDZ. Therefore, tell us, do you know that that spring in the towns around Vukovar the HDZ organised the so-called unarmed detachments?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I was interested in football. I don't know this. I wasn't interested in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know, did you hear that people started buying weapons at the time in an illegal way?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Sir, in our street, once the children came back from their summer vacation, we organised shifts, watching the situation. But our whole street had only one single rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is the name Slavko Dokmanovic familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes. The name is familiar to me. He was the president of the Trpinja football club. I played football, so I knew him. Also he worked for municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. That's the information I have, too, that he was involved in football. And this is how you knew him?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I will try to go back to correct something, but now I'm being told that, in fact, there is no error in the transcript, so we can move on. Would you please tell us what you did during the conflict in Vukovar? Were you mobilised or were you perhaps a volunteer with the National Guards Corps or in any other institution?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: In our street nobody was mobilised. I'm just telling you that we -- we had our watch shifts, that we had but one single rifle and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: After the Borovo Selo event, after the policemen were killed there, and once the children came back from their summer vacation. This is when the shelling started.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I suppose that you are referring to civilian protection, because this is what you mentioned in your statement, saying that you joined the civilian protection. My question was: When did you join the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: In late July.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the investigators you said late June, early July. Which is true?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Early August.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I am now going to refer to your statement. Do you have one in front of you? I will now ask the usher to give you a statement, your statement in Croatian. This is number 00327866. Will you please take a look at the first page, the first page with the text, which is actually the second page. The passage that starts with: "I will briefly set out my experience."

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: During the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. When it says here about the month.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: "I will briefly set out my experience during the conflict in Vukovar, which started following the deaths of several police officers in Borovo Selo in May that year. At the end of June and at the beginning of July I joined with other civilians, the civilian protection unit of the city of Vukovar. I did not join the National Guards Corps and I did not wear a uniform, but I did carry a rifle."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you agree with me that then, back then in 1995 your recollections were much better than they are today?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you see that when speaking of civilian protection you speak of late June, early July, so earlier then you said today. So can we then agree that as early as that you joined the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I have already told you that we joined the civilian protection once the children came back from their summer vacation and once the buses were shelled. Perhaps I misspoke that -- but that's when it was, and I'm telling you this frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. We will not dwell on this, but you will not be needing the statement for the time being. Keep it with you. What was your primary task? What did you do? You mentioned this in your statement, but since the Prosecutor didn't cover this with you, will you please tell us in detail what you did during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: During the conflict a friend of mine called Menges who was a schoolmate of mine, I was known to have nice handwriting, so he went with me to school at Sokak and I drew up lists of people who were in the basement so that food might be supplied to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you keep doing this throughout this time as the lists were being drawn up? Both you and Menges were doing this after all, as you said.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, Menges wasn't doing that. He was from -- he asked me and I was from Ivana Gorana Kovacica Street, and they asked me to help them with the lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you did, didn't you, you drew up those lists?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Just because I had such a fine handwriting they gave me those lists to be rite up for those people in basements to be given some food. All the food was being kept at the Hungarian school in a rather large hall, and it was from there that food was being distributed to the basements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You have mentioned that school already, the Hungarian school. Whereabouts was it exactly?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Just across the street in Radiceva Street facing Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was one of the defence headquarters there?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I don't know where Vukovar's defence headquarters were, but there was a group of armed people, our own people there. There was no need for me to carry a rifle or anything, because I was working in an office, but there were many basements there holding many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How many times did you draw up lists for them?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I worked at it for several days in a row. I would then go home, and every time I finished a list they would give me a new list, depending on who was in which basement. I cycled back to Radiceva Street because I myself lived on Ivana Gorana Kovacica Street. If you cycle, it takes about 10 or 12 minutes to reach the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You took several days to produce the list. What time would you say that was?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: That was in November, early November.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The first time you drew up a list was in early November, right?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your statement you pointed out that your principal duty was to produce these lists. What, then, had you been doing up to this point?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I was in my street and we stood guard just like everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Up to this point in time you had been standing guard. You weren't wearing any uniforms and you weren't carrying rifles, were you?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No uniform, but I did say that right from the word go we had a single rifle and we passed it on to the next person taking over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about later on? Later on you were given something, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: There was this one evening, I can't remember when exactly, but we were given a number of Kalashnikovs. We didn't get enough, because they'd given some to Sajmiste. We received those Kalashnikovs. We spent the whole night cleaning the rifles because they were oily and dirty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That presumes that you served in the army, right, and I expect you would be able to see if these were new?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, they were entirely new.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You were cleaning this rifles with this group of people. How many rifles were there?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Between 10 and 15, I'd say, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: These lists you've mentioned, what was done with these lists, eventually? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I don't know what was done with them, but I think Menges took the lists along to Zagreb on the break-through attempt.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I'm asking you. Because in your statement you said that Menges took the lists away from Zagreb -- from Vukovar and that he took them to Zagreb, which means it was some sort of a continuous action on his part?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I know that he had the lists on him during the break-through attempt, but his son was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know anything about a meeting that was held at the municipal building on Saturday, the 17th of November?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No. I know nothing about that meeting. When I gave the statement they asked me whether I had heard about that. It was upon my return that I heard about Vesna Bosanac holding a meeting of sorts. But during my three or four days at the hospital, I never actually met Vesna Bosanac. I never saw her.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you care to share with me what exactly you were told about this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I heard this when I was in Zagreb. I heard that Dr. Bosanac had been making proposals at the meeting, or whoever else was there, for the soldiers to put on white uniforms in order to save their lives. However, they chose not to and that proved to be a wise decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you claim you only learned about this in Zagreb later on, but you weren't there personally?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, nor did I see Dr. Bosanac over those last days, the three or four days that I spent at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but as you said today, you entered the hospital on the evening of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So do you allow for the possibility that a meeting was held before you got there on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I don't know. My wife and I were in the Velepromet basement. In the Velepromet basement. After we had escaped, we spent several days in the Velepromet basement across the way from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You personally?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, I personally, and my wife and people from Luzac who were also on the run and took refuge in those cellars.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your wife was a hospital employee. She was a dental specialist, a dentist, right?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes. My wife was a dentist with the hospital, and now she's a dental specialist, an orthodontist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: She was staying at the hospital all the time back then, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, not all the time. She would only go when she was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you left with her for the hospital. She wasn't at the hospital when you got there, nor was she sleeping at the hospital. Am I to take your words to mean that?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I spent several day with her in the Velepromet basement, as I've said already.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This means that at this point in time you left the previous place where you were?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes. We all fled our streets and went towards the hospital. Not straight to the hospital. We first stopped at this shelter, the warehouse that I told you about, and spent several days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this might be a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic [sic]. Could I mention for the benefit of Defence counsel that the evidence of the witness took just on one hour in chief. The cross-examination so far has extended for some half an hour. I would mention, I think, Mr. Domazet, I was thinking elsewhere and had your name wrongly; I apologise. I would suggest that Defence counsel might consider that the total cross-examination ought to be able to be concluded in about two hours between all three, If counsel would take that into account over the break. We will resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMRIDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMRIDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry to interrupt the proceedings. It's in relation to the next witness. At this time I have a very small application to make, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMRIDJIAN
utterances.text: The next witness has a little medical problem. One of his tooth was pulled out last night, and he is in some pain right now. He is under medication and he is asking if it's possible to start tomorrow morning instead of late this afternoon. I spoke to my learned friends, and they have some reservations about that, and they think that he should come and make that application himself. I leave it to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Your Honours, I may have sprung to my feet a little too quickly. As a matter of principle, the Defence would be well disposed to accept a motion like this. But we still believe that it would be all right for the witness to appear in person and to share his problems with us, just to make sure he is not ill again tomorrow. I seem to have found something about this witness that sort of rings a bell in some document or other, a document not likely to be used in these proceedings. We just believe it would be advisable for the Trial Chamber to get an impression on the witness's condition. Therefore, we move that the witness appear before the court in order to tell us himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMRIDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has already confirmed that he would be ready to start tomorrow, if that could help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A tooth was drawn, and when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMRIDJIAN
utterances.text: This happened just late afternoon yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I fear the application could mean that we would lose 40 minutes or so today. But given that there is a medical condition, a tooth has been drawn, this is the day after, we think that without undue inquiry, we can accept counsel's assurance of that matter. And we would allow the witness now to go and do whatever he can to recover, and we will hear the witness tomorrow morning. We continue in the morning tomorrow at 9.00, and it's not in this courtroom, it's in Courtroom II. So yes, you may work on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMRIDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That may give Mr. Lukic a little more time liberty, because if anybody needs some time with this witness, it may be Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will do my best to ensure that Mr. Lukic has sufficient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vilhelm, will you please take again the statement that should be before you? Please turn to page 1 of your statement and look at the portion with paragraph 8 beginning with the words: "In the municipal building." Would you please read out that entire passage?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: "A meeting was called at the municipal building to discuss what was going to happen. Dr. Bosanac attended the meeting and suggested that the defenders put on white coats and surrender to the occupying forces. The majority of the people refused this. As it turned out, it was a wise decision. This meeting took place on Saturday, the 17th of November."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. This is your statement given in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does this sound like something that you heard later, or is this description -- is this a description given by an eye-witness who was present and who heard who proposed what and who rejected what?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: There were people who testified before me in Zagreb and most likely they didn't understand this well. I said that I heard that there had been a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sir, you gave this statement, you read it, and you signed it. That's what you told us today.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that the statement does not say anywhere that you heard this in Zagreb, it doesn't say from whom you heard this, it doesn't explain to us how you learned this about who was present, what was going on, and so on.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: How would I know who was present? I never knew that, and I never heard about who had attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You have read out to us the second sentence where it says that Dr. Bosanac attended the meeting and made a suggestion for the defenders to put on white coats and surrender?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, this was discussed in Zagreb; therefore, I heard it. Dr. Bosanac was not with us in Zagreb. She was imprisoned in Sremska Mitrovica together with Dr. Njavro. This is what I heard from people who were with me at the Astoria hotel. And it's been a long time since 1995. This was discussed at the Astoria hotel where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You will agree with me that this is not what your statement says,, your statement doesn't say that you heard this from somebody else. It implies something else?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, let us read the paragraph starting with: "On the 19th of November."

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: "On the 19th of November, I went to the hospital where I spent the night with my wife with other medical staff. We slept on benches in an office in the basement."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That's enough. That's enough. So in 1995, you told us this today, your recollections were much better. You speak not only of the 19th of November, but also you say that you spent the night there. Today you told us it was on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I thought it was 19th, but actually we came on the 17th in the evening when it was raining. I spent three days at the hospital. I have no reason to lie. This is the correction that I am making. I arrived on the 17th in the evening. It was raining, the tanks were already by the railway station, and we had to move from the basement to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about the next paragraph? Will you please read out the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: "The next morning, on the 20th of November, the JNA soldiers and Chetniks entered the hospital."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You can stop there. Does this also imply that you could not have been mistaken when you said that after spending one night, on the following day you described what you did; namely, that the JNA came and so on. So how can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I can't explain this. I came on the 17th in the evening. When they asked me this, perhaps I didn't quite understand. There is no reason for me to lie to you. I came there on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Based on what you said today, you were at the hospital from the 17th until the 20th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that during that time you never saw Dr. Vesna Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No. I was in the basement with my wife and Dr. Kolak, the lady doctor who worked with my wife. The children were housed there in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that on the 19th you didn't see anyone either, the soldiers or anybody else. You just heard that somebody was at the hospital, but where you were, nobody came to inform you?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: We were at the children's ward. Nobody came to the children's ward. I didn't see anybody. We just heard what people were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You certainly know who Marin Vidic, Bili, was?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, I know Marin Vidic, Bili. I think that he is from Lovas and he used to work for the municipality as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you see him, perhaps, at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please wait for the end of the question and then give your answer? This is for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you didn't see him at the hospital during those days?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him at all during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about after the war? Did you hear what kind of a role he had during the war? You told us that you had heard some things from other people?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything. I just know that he had a good singing voice. I know that he was in Lovas. I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember what was happening at the hospital or what happened at the hospital from the moment you arrived on the 17th in the evening? Do you remember that something was taking place on the 17th in the evening at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, nothing. There were many wounded persons in the corridors. They were asking for help, there was no more medication, very little food. Nothing was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about on the 18th? Was something going on on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Whatever was going on, I was in the basement. I didn't leave the basement. My wife and I shared one bed. One would sleep for one hour and then the other one would sleep for one hour. We also had benches there. I didn't go outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that you did not go out on the 19th either, that you never left the premises in the basement until the 20th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I would go out into the corridors where I saw the wounded, some of them I recognised. They were on benches. Everything else was destroyed. There was no room for them in regular patient rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you arrived at the hospital, was that the only time that you came to the hospital during the war or did you come previously on some other occasions?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I came several times prior to that bringing the wounded from the Hungarian school to the hospital. When I was with Menges, Mr. Skoko and I - he had a car - brought the wounded to the hospital from the Hungarian school. They needed medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. Since you came to the hospital several times, do you remember whether the hospital was guarded? Were there any armed people guarding the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: At the entrance of the hospital where I would come with the wounded there was a soldier with a rifle guarding the entrance. I knew him, and I later heard that he was killed. His last name was Perkovic. I don't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say a soldier?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes. What I had in mind is that he wore a guard's uniform, and he stood there guarding the hospital with a rifle, checking who was going in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you see the same soldier every time you came to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I didn't go there many times. I came only once bringing in the wounded. I didn't go there more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you just read out to us the passage about the meeting held in the municipal building on Saturday, the 17th of November, what about that fact, that it was a Saturday? Did you learn that from people in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, most likely. I can't tell you now whether it was a Saturday or not. So many years have passed. Most likely it was the 17th. I know that the meeting was held. I know that it was raining. And at that meeting my son was present as well. Later on when he went into break-through, I learned from him that they had had a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. So this is a new element now.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I'm telling you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have concluded my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's appreciated indeed, Mr. Domazet. Yes, Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Mr. Vilhelm. My name is Mira Tapuskovic. I am one of the Defence counsel of Mr. Miroslav Radic. I will put very few questions to you.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We will comply with the instructions of the Trial Chamber to be brief. I would kindly ask you to make pauses before answering the questions so that the interpretation service has sufficient time to interpret timely and accurately what I say and what you say. Mr. Domazet asked you something about your statement which you gave in Zagreb in 1995.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was this statement given at the police station in Zagreb in the presence of investigators?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I don't know where it was. It was in a building in Zagreb. I don't even know what the building is called. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
