utterances.text: All right. Do you know in the meantime since then, and this was in 1995, did you give to anyone or any organisation, any other statement and did you submit anywhere a statement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, it didn't even occur to me. This was in 1995. And to tell you the truth, I even forgot that I had given a statement. It's been 10 years, madam. I didn't even reflect on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us about where you lived in Vukovar, what the profession of your wife is. Now, tell us this: In 1991, how old were your children, and what is their gender?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I told you that the occupation had just started when my son returned back from serving his military duty, which was in Tuzla. He came back in July, and he was supposed to go with the army to some front lines. However, somehow he managed to come home from Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said in your 1995 statement something about Menges. You said that his son got killed attempting to break through the siege. Do you remember his first name? Was it Vladimir Menges?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I believe so. Menges, the father, is a painter, house-painter.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you this.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I think that that was his profession.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let us both try to comply with the Court's instructions. Tell me, do you know what happened later to Menges?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I don't know. You mean the son?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The son got killed; you told us that.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: The father lives in Vukovar to this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was the father exchanged later on after being taken to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: He was not taken to Sremska Mitrovica. The father managed to escape in the break-through.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I had some information indicating that he was in Sremska Mitrovica, if his first name is indeed Vladimir.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: The Menges that I have in mind is the one who left the town through a break-through and went to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now that you are mentioning break-throughs, you told us that Mr. Menges had lists of persons who were in various shelters in Vukovar. Tell me, please, for you in civilian protection, was a break-through the only way of delivering these lists to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what was his task.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know that Dr. Bosanac sent daily appeals, pleading for assistance to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I don't know that, sir [as interpreted]. There was no electricity. I have no knowledge about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were involved in writing down the lists of residents and ensuring food supply?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Madam, I worked in a school building, we did not have a telephone, we did not have anything but a desk. All I did was copy these lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please remember to make breaks.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: All right. Do you want me to repeat this slowly?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No need. When asked by Mr. Domazet you told us something about the conditions under which these lists were made and when they were brought. Once the lists were submitted to Mr. Menges, were they updated later?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. I have no idea. All I know is that I wrote down the names of the people who were in basements in various streets.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, you did not update them once you wrote them down?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I never saw them again, these lists. I only saw them on the day when I copied them. And I copied them because they wanted this to be written out in a nice handwriting, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Even though you said that your only task was to copy the lists, and that was because you had a nice handwriting, you were still involved with the civilian protection. Can you tell us on what day was the police station hit and when was it set on fire?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you the exact date, but it was around the 16th or the 17th. I'm not sure though.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. But at any rate, you will agree with me that it was several days before -- would you please wait for me to complete my question. You will agree with me that it was several days before Vukovar fell?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were involved in civil protection. Did you ever meet anyone called Frano Kozul?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Frano Kozul, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I'm sorry, I just have to go through my questions again, because my learned friend Mr. Domazet asked some of the same questions that I had planned. If you remember, I believe you have a copy of your statement in front of you, I'm not about to quote you, but you did say that a break-through attempt had been organised for members of Vukovar's defence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: It was no organised thing, really, because the police had gone on before them. They heard that the police had started a break-through attempt, but not many of them got through, and they tried to do the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you have that statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the benefit of my learned friends, this is page 1 of the witness statement, paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please follow and confirm whether what I have just read out is accurate. "The break-through was an organised attempt to escape by the rather large number of people, for the most part those who had been at the defence positions." Is this an accurate quote, sir? Please wait for me. Is this an accurate quote from your statement?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You signed this statement back in 1995 to confirm that it was accurate and faithful, an accurate and faithful reflection of your account, the account that you gave at the time?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes. This is something that my son told me, because he was part of the break-through. The break-through was successful, and I heard that my son was alive, that he had survived. It was on the bus from Djakovo on our way to Zagreb. My son told me that the break-through had taken three days and that it was eventually successful.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have stated that you were a member of civil protection. And you have just read out yourself that the break-through was an organised attempt by a rather large number of people who had been at the defence positions. Can you agree then that in addition to your duties with the civil protection unit you had other duties to do with the town's defence. You did, after all, tell us that you carried a rifle, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I did carry a rifle, but in my own street, Ivana Gorana Kovacica Street, I drew up the guard schedule, both day-time and night-time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever meet someone named Stjepan Pole?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I know Stjepan Pole, but it's all because of football. He was a member of the police and I knew the man, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. About Stjepan Pole, after the clashes had erupted in Vukovar, did Stjepan Pole stay in Vukovar throughout and did you see him around?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I didn't go anywhere. I was at the school building and every now and then medical assistance had to be provided for a tooth extraction or something like that. It was under heavy shelling that we sometimes drove these people to the hospital to be helped.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So what was the real reason for you not joining the break-through attempt, since you were a member of Vukovar's defence forces?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Dear lady, I didn't even know about the break-through attempt. My son had come to see me and my wife four or five days previously. He came to the basement where we were staying. He wanted me to give him some money because he would not surrender to the Chetniks, and that's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where did your son come from?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: He was also staying at the Hungarian school. He was at those positions facing the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Having left the hospital and headed for the buses, did you put on white overcoats?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I didn't. I don't think anybody on the bus had white overcoats at all. Except maybe for the driver and perhaps two or three other people. There was no one else wearing either a military uniform or a white overcoat.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: None of the 20 or so people there?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Not on my bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm talking about your bus on the way from the hospital to the barracks. How many soldiers were there on the bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: You mean on the bus?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. That's what I'm asking about. Any soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, one. And the driver.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember how much time you spent inside the barracks on the bus? And this whole time, between your arrival at the barracks and your return to the hospital, how long did that take?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. We didn't stay at the barracks that long. A soldier came over, or whoever, I didn't actually see him, who brought a list containing the names of wives whose husbands were detained on that bus. They called out the names and whoever was on the bus went back to the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You mentioned Mihajlo Kolesar a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said he was a neighbour of yours.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I put it to you that Mr. Kolesar was interviewed by the OTP the same year as you and he clearly stated that he was wearing a white overcoat and that he was not the only one wearing a white overcoat, what would you say? Excuse me, sir, I am trying to find a reference. For the benefit of my learned friends from the OTP, this is page 5 of the B/C/S statement made by Mr. Kolesar. Would that perhaps refresh your memory to the effect that you, Mr. Kolesar, and perhaps someone else on that bus were, in fact, wearing white overcoats?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I don't remember. All I know is that Biba Kolesar was the head nurse. And he was not on my street throughout this time. He was at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But that wasn't my question, sir. Please, allow me to finish asking you my question. It's because of the interpretation. My question is: Do you think it would ring a bell with you if I told you that Mr. Kolesar said in a statement that he was wearing a white overcoat and this seems to suggest that he was not the only one wearing a white overcoat. Does that stir any memories, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: It can only mean that they were familiar with that meeting where Dr. Bosanac told them to put on white overcoats, because their wives were employees of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You dropped a couple of names in your testimony today, the names of persons on that bus. You just told us that you and Mr. Kolesar were neighbours?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We were neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What would you say if I told you that Mr. Kolesar was asked this question: "Did you know anyone on that bus?" And on the same page of his statement to the OTP back in 1995, he clearly stated that he didn't know anyone on that bus. What would you say, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: That's up to him. It's none of my business. All I know is that I took an oath before this Court and what I'm telling you is the truth, the naked truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you arrived here you prepared for this testimony. You told us that this is your first appearance before any court, and you clearly stated that you had no past forum. As you were being proofed for your testimony, were you shown a list?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I was shown a list of people I had seen at the hospital. The list from the bus --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you hold right there, please? What I asked you is whether you were shown a list. I didn't ask whether the list was in reference to the persons on the bus or the persons at the hospital. All I asked was were you shown a list?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I'm telling you, I didn't see any list at all. Only some people I recognised, if I had seen anyone at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That means on the 17th of February in The Hague you were shown a list with first and last names -- with the first and last names of certain persons?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you told what sort of list this was?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony today on page 22, line 20, you testified in chief about a person you recognised by the name of Ivan Adzaga?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I didn't say Ivan Adzaga. I just said Adzaga. I said I didn't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Further -- bear with me, please. I am putting together some notes here concerning the examination-in-chief of the witness. Likewise, concerning that list, the nature of which you were not informed about, you marked the name of Lovro Barbir?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: He was on the bus with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. You also mentioned some people named Medjesi and marked their names, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance with the pronunciation. There are two names in this list; it says "Medjesi" twice.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, father and son.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Father and son. All right. You said in your statement that this person was called Zoran Medjesi, whereas today on page 24 you marked Zoran Medjesi, whereas today on page 24, line 4 of the transcript, you said you didn't know the names of the Medjesis, the father and son.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Where in this statement can you find Zoran Medjesi?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I corrected myself. I said it was on that list that you marked. And probably someone added the word "bus" next to your name, the name Medjesi, and you said to us today, on page 24 that you didn't know the names of the Medjesis, father and son?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Father and son. Cigo was a waiter. There is only two males by the name of Medjesi, two men. These are the only two Medjesis that I know of. Their wife [as interpreted] is Verica Medjesi.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I just have another question. You said that you were reunited with your family on the 25th and 26th of November in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: My son only. My son.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Your statement says your family, the 25th and the 26th of November. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: When I said "family," I meant my son, because my daughter remained in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, sir. My name is Novak Lukic, Defence counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin. I will be asking a number of questions now. I am happy with the pace of the cross-examination, but as my learned friends have already asked you, the problem is, we understand each other as we speak, but the interpreters must hear both me and you. It's for the sake of the transcript. So, please, if could you pause after my question.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I'm a bit quick by nature. I tend to jump the gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So am I; that's no problem at all. The first question, I usually start with something involving my client. You described the situation where Sljivancanin was talking to Vujovic on behalf of all of you. Could you just wait a minute, sir? And you described how you found out that the person in question was Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember about that day? Except for this meeting after your return from the barracks, did you see Sljivancanin again?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: When I returned from the hospital, for the first time in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my understanding, but I just wanted to make sure. There is another question that I have to ask you by way of clarification to make sure how I should interpret your testimony. You were asked in chief about your posts and positions. You're familiar with the structure of the JNA, with the TO. From your time with the JNA, you were also familiar with the various ranks and the general structure. My question about this is: You used the term "Chetnik" here today. When you say "Chetnik," what do you mean? Do you include the JNA in that definition, or do you mean the volunteers, the TO, Seselj's men and such-like?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Dear, sir, I know very well what a regular army is. To be quite honest, I did not see any Chetniks there. I saw a number of reservists, but I did not see any Chetniks, and I'm thankful for that. No real Chetniks at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I fully understand that. But you kept using the term Chetniks, so what exactly did you mean? The reservists or active duty JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I meant the reservists. The reservists from Vukovar who put on the military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am much clearer about it now. Thank you. A few very brief questions. Let me just check. You answered some of them. You were in the hospital from the 17th on, and during those several days that you spent at the hospital, among or from your fellow citizens did you hear that civilians who were not the wounded and who were not members of the medical staff should go to Velepromet rather than go to the hospital? Did you hear anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, I didn't ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, do you know that in those last few days there was a large influx of civilians coming to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will now turn to the 20th -- but, rather, another question concerning the 19th. You said that you didn't see any JNA members. Did you hear, perhaps, when talking to the people at the hospital, whether on the 19th the International Red Cross and some journalists came, perhaps, to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, I never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask you to remember something which might prove difficult for you, and if that is the case, please say so. On the 20th in the morning how late was it when they told you to leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I can't remember that. All I know is that we leaned against the wall and we had to put our arms up and that they frisked us to see if we had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you were leaving the hospital, your wife was asked to come to a meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was. My wife and I split while we were still in the basement. They were informed that all hospital staff had to go to this meeting. Until my return from the barracks, I didn't see my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. That's what I understood it to be the case [as interpreted]. Did your wife perhaps later on tell you how long that meeting went on for?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us just now, you even showed how they frisked you, how they searched you. Tell us, please, so that all of us here know, what were they looking for, the soldiers who were searching you?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: The soldiers who were searching us were looking for weapons. They frisked us all over, our trousers and the upper body as well. That's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have it recorded in the transcript that the witness showed on himself exactly how they frisked them.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, please tell me this, if you can: From the moment you came out, and we here in the courtroom have quite a clear picture, because we saw some photographs of that area, you went out through the back door where the corridor is, where the tunnel is, so you went out through that door. From the moment you went out, until you boarded the buses, how much time elapsed?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I couldn't say. They searched us and it didn't take a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So if I were to say 15 minutes, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I can't say. I can't remember. We got on the buses, one by one. I boarded the second bus and that's what I stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's try it this way: If I described in these terms, after you were searched did you stay there waiting in the column or did you go to the bus immediately after you were searched?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, no. That didn't take a long time because there were not that many of us. And then we went from the hospital to the buses. The buses were parked on the other side, near the back door of the hospital towards the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned several times today the people that you recognised, who boarded the bus together with you, the second bus coming out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These persons, were any of them wounded or patients or were they perhaps hospital employees or civilians?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Jakov Simunovic, Sime, was a hospital employee. Sime senior was the driver for the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the others? Were any of them patients?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: None of the people that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember the buses were parked there. You said that there were between three and five buses. Did they differ from each other in terms of colour, size, or were the buses similar to each other?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I couldn't say whether these were JNA buses, I can't remember. At any rate, they were lined one after the other. I can't remember, no. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's continue. Can you tell us, from the moment you boarded the bus how much time passed before the buses set off?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I couldn't say, but it wasn't long. We moved in the direction towards Sajmiste where the barracks was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the period of time.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I couldn't say, but it didn't take long.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it more than half an hour?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: It wasn't more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether during that period of time, while you were still waiting on the buses, any soldiers or officers got on the bus to tell you that those who had hospital IDs should get off the bus. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anybody get off the bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I don't know that. I know that Jakov Simunovic and some others said that they had their IDs and showed them, whereas some people said that they had forgotten their IDs and didn't have them on them. Those who had hospital IDs, they showed them, and there were some who were employed at the hospital but didn't have the IDs on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When asked by the Prosecutor you said that you remembered Martin Dosen lying on a stretcher.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No. I didn't see Martin Dosen lying on a stretcher, no. I saw him at the hospital near the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when did you see Martin Dosen at the hospital near the entrance?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I saw Martin at the hospital in the morning. I know everybody in Vukovar, and later on I heard that he had saved Stanislav Avramovic during the war. He transferred him to Rakic's, and this is how he saved his live. Stanislav Avramovic was at the hospital. He asked him for help, but he didn't help him. He said, "Later." I saw Avramovic in front of the hospital too. We used to play football together. I was his coach. He doesn't dare return to Vukovar now. He's now living in America.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we heard some testimony about that. So you didn't see Martin Dosen in front of a bus?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember whether all of you on your bus were sitting or was perhaps anybody standing while they were driving you to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Nobody stood on my bus. I don't know about the other buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another question: Do you remember as you were approaching the buses, did you board the buses randomly or were all of you told exactly which bus to board?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, we boarded them randomly. Nobody told us which bus to board.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, let us turn to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us that all the buses came together parked in a semi-circle?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, one behind the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. If you were already asked this, I apologise, but tell me, this mistreatment when the people came to your buses, started threatening you, had rifles and so on, did it go on the whole time until you transferred in to another bus or not?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, only in the beginning when the buses just arrived. Nobody tried to defend us. They came to the buses, had rifles there and started shouting, "You ought to be killed," and so on. This was an enraged mob, mob out of control. They had rifles, pistols; however, not a single bullet was fired, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We heard testimony here, and you will tell me if this is correct or not, Jakov Simunovic said that this lasted for 10 or 15 minutes and then they calmed down.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to say whether it was 10 or 15 minutes, but I can tell you that it didn't last very long. Not long. Sir, let me tell you frankly. I was scared. I didn't look around. The soldiers and reservists who were outside, they were looking to see if they could recognise somebody on a bus. They were looking for familiar faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And based on your testimony, those were mostly local residents of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I told you before that I recognised only two soldiers wearing military uniforms. They were reservists. Dule Robija, Dusko Vojnovic, nicknamed Robija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right, that's one name. Do you remember the other person?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: The other person is nicknamed Kum. While I played for Sloga, I knew him. He's not a normal person. He's not quite all right up there, and he used to live in Negoslavci. He was at the entrance to the barracks with a weapon. He is a crazy person. What can be said about him?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I need the assistance of the usher. Do you have your statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will read just a brief passage from your statement. English version page 3, paragraph 5. For you it's paragraph 4. It begins with the words: "After some time." Would you now please read this: "In order to get to the buses." Would you please read it out slowly?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: "After some time, somebody came to the bus with a list of names who were called out. My name was among them. I got off the bus and was directed towards an empty bus. I was the first to get on that bus. People got off other buses and came to the bus that I was on. In order to get to the bus, they had to walk between two lines of Chetniks or run a gauntlet. These people beat them with trunches and rifle-butts. Kolesar was badly beaten. At the time he was saying, 'I'm a Ruthenian,' so not a Russian, but a Ruthenian, 'I had nothing to do with the war.' Another person who was beaten was Jakov Simunovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's enough. I wanted you to read this in order to clarify something. I suppose that you are here to reaffirm what you had stated to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is why I asked you at the outset what you meant when you said "Chetniks," because here you used the word "Chetnik" to describe those who beat people who were going on the bus. Therefore, did you mean that those were reservists from Vukovar, these Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I don't know who beat the people. There were civilians among them, reservists and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another sentence that you uttered today, when asked by the Prosecutor on page 12, line 24 whether you saw who was beaten as they were moving from one bus to the other, you said, "I put my head down. I didn't see, but I heard them beat Simunovic."

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I stated and I can confirm that. He was across from me. I put my head down because I was terrified. I didn't look around. I just heard moans. I heard that they were beaten. That they were being beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I never discussed it with them in Zagreb or at any other time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please just describe this man by the name of Dule Robija? Can you remember his physical appearance, what he looked like?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Of course I can. We played football together. I helped him. I played with Rijeka, with Borovo, and with Dinamo Vinkovci. He was a very, very good footballer. A very, very good one. I helped him to become the right back with Borovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want to know about his physical appearance.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I don't know, but he wasn't very tall. And later on, when I returned to Vukovar, I was with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he younger than you?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, a great deal younger.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Blond, dark?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Blond, small.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us about your return from the barracks to the hospital, you told us about meeting my client and Miroljub Vujovic. I will share with you the position of my client right off. I believe the OTP may be interested in this. Mr. Sljivancanin says it's quite correct that Miroljub Vujovic was there and some other TO people he didn't know. But this is not something that you need to know about.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Darko Kovacevic was there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you the following question: Were I to tell you that in relation to each and every one of you who were there, Sljivancanin asked Miroljub Vujovic what he knew about all of you and whether you had taken part in combat, and then Miroljub Vujovic would say that someone did, for example, and this person was sent back to the bus. Do you agree with what my client claims?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I don't know about the others. I know about myself. Miroljub Vujovic said I had been a loyal citizen of Vukovar up to a point in time, after which point in time my son and I allegedly became Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he say this about your son too, that your son had been involved with Vukovar's defence?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: They knew all, they knew it all, sir. They -- he said that my son was an Ustasha and that I was too. Which we weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean the locals from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, sir. That's precisely who I mean, the locals from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One question to wrap it up. I asked you something about Martin Dosen. You said you had seen him in the hospital. He was inside the hospital, as a matter of fact. My question: You didn't see him on that day on the 20th on any sort of stretcher anywhere, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it seems that we have been quite effective today, all of us, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a wonderful sign of things to come. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vilhelm, can I just ask you one or two questions, please? You told us that when you went to the hospital you saw a guard at the gate and his name was Petkovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: No, sir, Mr. Judge, not Petkovic, Perkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's not the Judge speaking on this occasion; it's the Prosecution counsel.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] Perkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Perkovic, P-e-r-k-o-v-i-c. You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, how did you know Mr. Perkovic?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Perkovic because he was my daughter's friend. They were schoolmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And your daughter, do you know the year that your daughter was born? I don't want to know her date of birth; that's impossible for most fathers. But do you know the year when your daughter was born?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: My daughter was born in 1966.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like you, if you would be kind enough, please, to look at the list that you have been shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing I would like to ask you. The reference -- I'm not sure about the subject matter. I may be jumping the gun on this one, but I have no idea which of us referred to this on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It was put by Mr. Domazet in cross-examination. There was cross-examination on his statement and there was reference and indeed the question was, was there -- was anyone on the gate, if my memory serves me correctly, and that's when the name was given. I see Mr. Domazet nodding in agreement with that. Thank you very much. I wonder if we could have it in focus, please, starting with M and ending at P.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, do you see that, Mr. Vilhelm?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The letter M, Medjesi, Andrija, and Medjesi, Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But I don't want you to look at that part. I would like you to look right at the very bottom.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: What else then?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I am going to hopefully tell you. There are three names of Perkovic, Damija, Jusef and Stjepan. Now, you've told us --

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I think it's Perkovic, Josip, but I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honours. But the last name that's been read out isn't Perkovic. It's Petrovic, Stjepan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said Josip Perkovic and Stjepan Petrovic -- Perkovic, Josip is the second to last; and Stjepan Petrovic is the last name on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And which one do you think was the guard at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: When they came to the hospital who was there? Well, just a student with a uniform. He was standing there stopping people on the way out when they were taking the wounded out, and he was probably guarding the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vilhelm, will you just listen to the question for a moment, if it's possible? You've told us about this young man being friendly with your daughter. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: That's Josip Perkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, can I deal with Josip Perkovic? Well, perhaps I can leave the question in relation to that. I want to move on. There is a certain writing on that document, but I want to deal with your statement for a moment. You have been asked by Mr. Domazet about your statement. And you have been asked about various parts of it.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told that the following document is in the e-court system. It is 04668267. And I suppose the best way of describing it is an addendum to the witness statement that was originally compiled in 1995. I wonder if that could be placed on the screen, please? Has anybody got that on their screen? I certainly don't. Shall I repeat the number? 04668267, 268. Your Honour, I still don't have it. Perhaps we can see if we've got it in Sanction and we can try and sort it out in Sanction. Well, I have the document now, but I've only part of the document. I wonder, is it possible for the document to be put in a way that I can actually read part of it? I've got the B/C/S and then I've got half of the English. Is there any way that that can be put in a way that can be read, please? I've got -- it's not in focus and I cannot read it. Now I can read it, but I can only read half of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It can be moved progressively up, if you would like that, until you reach what you want to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. I wonder, then, if that's the case, perhaps the best starting port is 8268 and we'll go to the very bottom of that, which is a signature. I also happen to have a hard copy, if that helps, to give to the witness. That's page 1 of 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, can you see that particular item on the screen? Do you see a signature -- did you see a signature there?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes. The 18th of January, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me one moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have got a date, the 18th of the 1st, 2006 on that particular page. And can we look at the other page, please? Can we scroll down to the bottom? Again, that signature, is that your signature on the page? Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes. It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you have been asked various questions about your statement and you were asked really in relation to three topics. Do you remember that you were asked about Dr. Bosanac and the fact that you had said in your statement that Dr. Bosanac had told people to put on white coats? Do you remember that question being asked of you?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at this particular document and we scroll up to the top of it - thank you - and can we move across so we can see the English? Can we scroll across even more, please? Well, I'll deal with it as best I can, because I have not got it all on my screen. But is it right to say that when you were seen by people from the Office of the Prosecutor you indicated to them, I think it was actually in December, but you signed the document on the 18th of the 1st, 2006, that in actual fact you never heard Dr. Bosanac say these words, it was only later on you learnt that there were some individuals in the hospital who put them on, white coats? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: That's true. I found out later, I heard from my son who was at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Vasic had an objection. No, he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us move then please to the next question. The question was in respect of the final paragraph of your statement that you had said "on the 19th of November I went to the hospital." Can we scroll down, please, to what I will call the second amendment? Is it right to say, again, that when you saw representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor you amended that to saying that it should not be the 19th, it should be the 17th?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: That's true. I did say that and I'm ready to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And just -- there were two other amendments. Can we just deal with one final one? Can we scroll down, please, to perhaps page 2 of 2, if that's possible? 268. Again, I just -- I can't read mine at all. If we deal with the questions in relation to your statement, you were asked about the page number, 27868. It says: "The next morning of the 20th" in the statement, is it right in your addendum, you said that it should be replaced with the words: "In the morning of the 20th." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: That's right. Accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And perhaps we've got it already, if we can just scroll down one more time to the next correction, please. The words in your statement that: "I'm Russian." And in actual fact what it was was "rusins," and that was an amendment that was put in in January?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes. I think Kolesar was a Ruthenian from Petrovac. He had a brother who was a Ruthenian, that much is certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So in actual --

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In actual fact, the statement that was taken from you was in 1995, these amendments were made in 2006, signed in 2006 in January. Did any member of the Office of the Prosecutor ever approach you in between that time to check the accuracy of your statement?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: When they came to see me, I told them everything was accurate. The statement I gave -- the amendments, rather, that I meant, I said that everything was now accurate and that this was the only real thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And was that the first opportunity you had had to change your statement?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: That was the first opportunity when they came to see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: In actual fact ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can I just deal with one other matter. I'd like to deal with the list that has been used by the Defence and which I have referred to. I wonder if it can be put, it's on Sanction, can it be put on to the screen, please? Thank you very much. I've got it very clearly now. Has everybody else got it? Thank you. Now, I don't want to go through the complete detail of every name, but can we just work out exactly what occurred when you came to The Hague? Is it right that you came The Hague, I believe, last Thursday, I think that was the 16th of February. Is that right or not? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I spent the night in Zagreb, and the next day I left for The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what day did you arrive at The Hague? I don't need a date, just approximately.

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Friday. I don't know the date. It was a Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, can we just deal with what occurred here at The Hague? Is it right that you were spoken to by the young lady who sits on my right, Ms. Regue? Can you just look over here for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is it right that she spoke to you about your statement?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: That's right. She spoke to me about your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And with regard to the discussion she had with you, is it right that you were asked to remember the names of the people who travelled with you on the bus to the JNA barracks and the bus that returned to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can we just move on in time? If we just deal with today, which is the 23rd, you have given evidence today for the first time. Is it correct that you saw me yesterday for the first time, discussing your evidence? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it is not quite right to ask these leading questions, when did you see me for the first time. It is just too leading in nature. It's not about the subject matter. We are not objecting to that, but we believe a little more caution when asking the questions would be called for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Of course I will do it that way if my learned friend wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember when it was that you had a meeting with me about your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: It was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And which day was that?

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: I don't know. It's difficult for me to remember the exact day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I am going to lead, and the -- was it yesterday morning --

utterances.speaker: RUDOLF VILHELM
utterances.text: Monday, perhaps. Yesterday -- it wasn't yesterday. It wasn't yesterday morning. I was here yesterday. I was waiting to appear in the courtroom from at about 3.00 yesterday. But I didn't even see the gentleman yesterday. I didn't get to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. I'll not take -- I'll not deal with this matter any further. I have to deal with it another way, if I may, which may require me giving a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Moore. You will be pleased to know, Mr. Rudolf, that that concludes the questions -- Mr. Vilhelm, that the counsel have for you. That the Chamber would like to thank you for your trouble in coming to The Hague and for the assistance you have been able to give us. Now, you are now, of course, able to return to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to thank the Chamber for hearing me out. Thank you very much to all those who heard me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, we've been taken a little by surprise with time. In the circumstances, we must adjourn now for the evening. We resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in number two court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 24th day of February, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.42 p.m.,
